Foundations: Who You Serve and How Clients Arrive

Before sending a single message, you need to know how a stranger becomes a paying client, exactly who you are looking for, and what you will say you do. This module also gets your profile, proof and safety habits ready so that the first prospect who checks you out finds a professional.

Many skilled women in service businesses, such as bookkeepers, caterers, designers, tailors who take corporate orders and social media managers, are good at the work but get clients only by chance: a cousin recommends them, a church member calls, then nothing for weeks. **Client acquisition** is the deliberate, repeatable process of finding people who need your service, starting conversations with them, and turning the right ones into paying clients. It is a separate skill from the service itself, and like any skill it can be learned and practised.

This course is for people who sell a **service to other businesses or professionals**, often called B2B (business to business). Selling to a school, a clinic, a hotel or a busy lawyer is different from selling tomatoes in the market: fewer buyers, bigger orders, longer decisions, and the relationship matters more than the single sale. If you sell products to everyday shoppers, the WODDI course on customer relations and sales is the better companion.

The five stages of the pipeline
Think of your clients as moving through a pipe. Every client you have ever had went through these stages, even if it happened quickly and by accident:
**Prospect:** a specific business or person who could need your service. Example: 'Grace Pharmacy on Ogui Road, which posts on Instagram but has no price list online.'
**Conversation:** they have replied to you or you have spoken. A reply of any kind, even 'not now', moves them here.
**Qualified:** you have checked that they have a real need, can pay, can decide (or can bring the decider), and want it soon enough to matter.
**Proposal:** you have sent a clear offer with scope, price and timing.
**Client:** they have agreed in writing and paid a deposit or the full fee.

Each stage has fewer people than the one before, so you must start with more prospects than the clients you want.
Inbound and outbound

**Inbound** means clients come to you: someone sees your WhatsApp status, finds you on Google Maps, or is referred by a happy client. **Outbound** means you go to them: you research a business and send a personal message, visit their office, or ask a mutual contact for an introduction. Inbound feels comfortable but is slow and unpredictable for a new business. Outbound is something you can do on Monday morning and measure by Friday. This course focuses mostly on outbound, plus referrals, because those are the parts you control.

Working backwards from a target

Because every stage loses people, you can work out how much outreach you need. You do not need perfect numbers at the start: begin with a cautious guess, then replace it with your own real numbers after a month (Lesson 3.3 shows how).
Worked example: how many messages for 2 new clients a month?

For example, Ngozi runs a small bookkeeping service in Enugu. She wants 2 new monthly clients. She guesses cautiously that out of every 10 personal messages, 3 people reply, 1 of those 3 agrees to a call, and half of her calls become clients.
Clients wanted per month: 2.
Calls needed: 2 clients divided by 0.5 (half of calls convert) = 4 calls.
Replies needed: 4 calls multiplied by 3 (one call for every 3 replies) = 12 replies.
Messages needed: 12 replies divided by 0.3 (3 replies per 10 messages) = 40 messages.
Per week: 40 messages divided by 4 weeks = 10 messages, which is 2 per working day.
Ngozi needs about 40 well-researched messages a month, roughly 2 every weekday, to expect 2 new clients. That is a small, achievable daily habit rather than a vague hope.
Your numbers will differ

The 3 in 10 reply rate above is a planning guess, not a fact about the market. Warm contacts (people who know you) usually reply far more often than strangers. Track your own results and update the calculation.
Where are you stuck?

Look at your last three months honestly. If you have almost no prospects, you are stuck at stage 1 and need Lesson 2.1. If you message people but hear nothing, your outreach needs work (Lesson 2.2). If you have lots of friendly chats that never become paid work, you are not qualifying or proposing clearly (Lessons 2.3 and 4.1). Naming the stuck stage tells you which part of this course to study hardest.

'I do social media for anybody who needs it' sounds flexible, but it makes client acquisition very hard. You cannot search for 'anybody', you cannot write a message that fits everybody, and a busy business owner cannot tell whether you understand her problem. The solution is an **ideal client profile (ICP)**: a short description of the kind of client you serve best and can find easily.

The **trigger** is the part most people forget, and it is often the most useful. A trigger is a visible event that creates a need: a restaurant opening a second branch needs staff uniforms; a school before admissions needs flyers and social media posts; a company at year end needs its books tidied for tax filing. When you see the trigger, you know who to contact and why now.

Choose a profile you can reach

Good ICPs are based on evidence, not wishes. Ask yourself: Where have my best past clients come from? Which industry do I understand from my own life or past jobs? Where can I find a list of these businesses (Google Maps, an association directory, a market, a church or mosque business directory)? A nurse who now offers bookkeeping might choose small private clinics because she understands how they run. That background is a real advantage in conversations.
The search test

Type your profile into Google Maps or Instagram search, for example 'nursery school Kaduna'. If you can find at least 30 real businesses in under 20 minutes, your profile is specific and reachable. If you find 3, widen it. If you find 3,000 with no way to tell them apart, narrow it.
Write a one-sentence offer

Your offer sentence explains what you do in terms of the **result** the client gets, not the tasks you perform. A useful pattern is: **I help [ideal client] get [result] by [how], so they [benefit].** Keep it under 30 words and avoid words like 'quality', 'excellent' and 'affordable' which every competitor uses.
Worked example: from vague to specific
For example, Halima in Kaduna manages social media. Her old description was 'I do social media management, graphics and content for businesses at affordable prices.'
She chose an ICP: private nursery and primary schools in Kaduna with 100 to 400 pupils, run by the proprietor, before each admissions season.
She listed the result schools care about: more parent enquiries during admissions.
She described how: 3 posts a week showing real classroom life, plus WhatsApp-ready flyers parents can forward.
She wrote: 'I help Kaduna nursery and primary schools get more parent enquiries before each admissions season, with weekly posts and forwardable flyers that show real classroom life.' (26 words)
Halima now knows who to search for, when to contact them, and what to say in her first line. Her offer is specific enough that a proprietor can say 'yes, that is us' within seconds.
A person searching through profiles with a magnifying glass
A clear profile turns 'anybody' into a short list of businesses you can actually look up.
Add a starter offer

A new client is taking a risk on you. A **starter offer** is a small, clearly priced first job that lets them test you before a bigger commitment. It is not free work. Examples: a one-month social media trial with 12 posts; a one-off clean-up of three months of records; a tasting menu for a company's end-of-month staff lunch. Price it fairly so it covers your time and costs, and explain what happens next if they are happy.
Small enough to say yes to quickly, usually one decision-maker can approve it alone.
Big enough to show real results the client can see.
Clearly scoped: what is included, what is not, and the deadline.
Leads naturally to an ongoing or larger service.
Avoid working free to 'prove yourself'

Free work attracts people who do not value your time and rarely leads to paid work. If you want to lower the risk for a client, use a small paid starter offer, a clear money-back condition you can afford, or examples from past work instead.
You can have more than one ICP over time, but start with one for this course. Every lesson that follows, from building your list to writing messages, works better when it is aimed at one clear group.

Getting outreach-ready: profile, proof and safety
Set up a business profile that answers a prospect's first questions
Prepare simple proof of your work that is honest and shareable
Decide your price range before you start conversations
Apply basic safety rules against scams and fake clients

When you message a prospect, the first thing many will do is check you: they tap your WhatsApp profile, search your name on LinkedIn or Instagram, or ask someone. In a few seconds they decide whether you look real and capable. Getting ready before outreach means that check works in your favour. You do not need a website or a big following. You need three things: a clear profile, a little proof, and a price range you are confident about.
1. A profile that answers first questions

Use the **WhatsApp Business** app (free) rather than your personal WhatsApp for client work. It lets you add a business name, category, description, address, hours and a catalog, and it keeps work chats separate from family chats. On LinkedIn, which many professionals and corporate buyers use, make your headline say who you help and how, not just your job title.
**Photo:** a clear, friendly photo of you or a clean logo.
**Name:** your business name, spelled the same everywhere.
**Description:** your one-sentence offer from Lesson 1.2.
**Contact details:** a working email, your area or address if clients visit, and hours.
**Catalog or featured section:** 2 to 4 examples of your work or your starter offer.
2. Simple, honest proof

Proof reduces the risk a prospect feels. It does not need to be fancy. Good proof for a new business includes: before and after photos of your work, a short written summary of a past job (what the problem was, what you did, what changed), a screenshot of a genuine thank-you message shared **with the client's permission**, or a sample you made specially to show your style. Only use real work. If you are new, a well-made sample clearly labelled 'sample' is honest and still persuasive.
A person arranging work samples on a board
Two to four honest examples are enough proof to start outreach.
3. Know your price range before you talk

Many women lose confidence when a prospect asks 'how much?' early. Decide in advance. Calculate your costs and the time a typical job takes, then set a range for your starter offer and for your main service. You will adjust after qualifying (Lesson 2.3), but you should never be caught guessing. The WODDI pricing courses show the full costing method.
Worked example: a ready-to-say price range
For example, Chioma is a graphic designer in Port Harcourt targeting restaurants. Her starter offer is a menu redesign. Prices below are illustrative only.
She estimates the work: 6 hours of design plus 1 hour of revisions = 7 hours.
She values her time at about ₦5,000 per hour (approximate): 7 x ₦5,000 = ₦35,000.
She adds about ₦5,000 for data, software and printing a proof: ₦40,000.
She sets her range: about ₦40,000 for a simple one-page menu, up to about ₦60,000 for a multi-page menu with photo editing.

When a restaurant manager asks, Chioma can say calmly: 'A one-page menu redesign is usually around ₦40,000, and multi-page menus up to about ₦60,000. Once I see your current menu I can confirm the exact price.'
4. Safety before you start
Outreach means talking to strangers, and some strangers are not genuine. Scammers sometimes pose as large clients to steal money, data or free work. Use these rules from day one:
Before you accept a new client
Business exists and is findable
Talked to a real person
Scope agreed in writing
Deposit received in your account
No upfront fee asked of you
If any box stays unticked, pause before you start work.
Never pay a 'registration', 'vendor' or 'processing' fee to get a contract. Genuine clients pay you, not the other way round.
Confirm money has actually arrived in your bank app before starting. Screenshots of transfers can be faked.
Check that a business is real: look it up on Google Maps, its social pages, or the CAC public search for registered companies.
Meet new clients in public places or their real business premises during the day, and tell someone where you are going.
Never share your BVN, card PIN, OTP codes or passwords with a client.
Protect your accounts

Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp (Settings, Account, Two-step verification) and on your email. If someone asks you to read back a code you received by SMS, it is almost certainly an attempt to take over your account.
With a clear profile, a few honest examples, a ready price range and these safety habits, you are ready for the real work of Module 2: finding and contacting specific prospects.

Thirty well-researched prospects are worth more than three hundred phone numbers copied from a group. This lesson shows where to find them and how to record them so nothing gets lost.

Warm introductions

Start with your **warm network**, people who already know you. Write down 20 names of people you know who either fit your ideal client profile or work somewhere that does. Warm contacts reply more often and can introduce you to the decision-maker. Then add cold prospects from public sources until you reach 30.
A woman searching on a large screen
Spend your research time on a few businesses you understand well, not on hundreds of random numbers.
What to record for each prospect
Use a Google Sheet, Excel or even a notebook with columns. A spreadsheet is better because you can sort and filter later. Keep these columns:
Business name and location
Contact person and role (owner, manager, HR, procurement)
Where you found them and how to reach them (WhatsApp, email, LinkedIn, visit)

Respect personal data

Only record business contact details that the business itself has made public, or that someone gave you with permission. Do not copy members' numbers from private WhatsApp groups to message them for business. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 expects personal data to be collected and used fairly and for a clear purpose. Keep your sheet private, and delete people who ask you to stop contacting them.
Score prospects so you start with the best

Give each prospect a simple score from 0 to 3, one point for each of: **clear need** (you can see a problem you solve), **can pay** (the business looks established, has premises or steady activity), **reachable decider** (you can find the owner or manager). Contact the 3s first, then 2s. Leave 0s and 1s for later or drop them.
Worked example: researching 5 prospects in 40 minutes

For example, Bisi runs a catering service in Ikeja, Lagos, targeting offices with 20 to 80 staff that order lunch for monthly meetings. She opens Google Maps and searches 'offices Allen Avenue Ikeja' and 'co-working space Ikeja'.
Prospect 1: a co-working space with 4.5-star reviews where several reviews mention 'no food options'. Need yes, can pay yes, manager named on LinkedIn yes. Score 3.
Prospect 2: a law firm with a website listing 12 lawyers. Need unclear, can pay yes, office manager not found. Score 1.
Prospect 3: an insurance broker whose Instagram shows a monthly staff award event. Need yes, can pay yes, HR officer found on LinkedIn. Score 3.
Prospect 4: a small printing shop with 3 staff. Need low, can pay unclear. Score 0, outside her profile.
Prospect 5: a training centre whose posts mention weekend workshops of 40 people. Need yes, can pay yes, contact is the general WhatsApp line only. Score 2.
In 40 minutes Bisi has two score-3 prospects with a specific reason to contact each, one score-2 for this week, and two she can set aside. Repeating this six times gives her 30 researched prospects.

Writing personal outreach messages that get replies
Structure a short outreach message in four parts
Personalise each message using your research observation
Ask for one small, easy next step
Choose the right channel and timing for each prospect

Business owners receive many messages a day. A generic 'Hi, I do graphic design, let me know if you need anything' is easy to ignore because it asks the reader to do the thinking. A good outreach message does the thinking for them: it shows you noticed something specific, offers something useful, and asks for one small step. It should be readable in under 30 seconds on a phone.
The four-part message
Four parts of an outreach message
Personal opening
Specific observation
Useful offer
One small ask
Each part earns the right to the next, and the whole message stays under about 100 words.
**Personal opening:** greet by name, and say how you know of them or who referred you. 'Good morning Mrs Okafor. Ada from Sunshine Pharmacy suggested I reach out.'
**Specific observation:** one sentence from your research that shows you looked. 'I saw that your new Wuse branch opens next month.'

**Useful offer:** connect your service to their situation in one or two sentences, with a result. 'I design price lists and shelf labels for pharmacies, which helps customers find products without queuing to ask.'
**One small ask:** a low-effort next step with a yes or no answer. 'Would it be useful if I sent two sample label designs for your new branch this week?'
A phone showing a message being sent
A short, specific message that asks for one small step is easier to say yes to.
Small asks win replies

Asking a stranger 'Can we sign a contract?' in your first message is too big a jump. Asking 'Can I send you two free samples?' or 'Would a 10-minute call on Thursday work?' is small, and a yes moves them into the conversation stage. Good small asks include: sending a short sample or idea, a 10 to 15 minute call, a quick visit to see their space, or a question about their current process.
Worked example: rewriting a weak message

For example, Chioma, the Port Harcourt designer from Lesson 1.3, is contacting a restaurant whose Instagram menu photos are blurry and hard to read. Her first draft was: 'Hello, I am a graphic designer. I do logos, flyers, menus and more. Contact me if you need anything. Thanks.'
Opening: 'Good afternoon Mr Tamuno, I am Chioma, a designer here in Port Harcourt. I enjoy following Riverside Grill on Instagram.'
Observation: 'I noticed your menu photo on your latest post is hard to read on a phone, especially the prices.'
Offer: 'I redesign restaurant menus so they are clear on phones and print well, which can save staff time answering price questions on WhatsApp.'
Ask: 'Would you like me to send a quick mock-up of your top section, so you can see the difference? No obligation.'
Word count: 74 words, readable in about 20 seconds.

The new message proves she looked, names a benefit the owner cares about, and asks for a yes that costs him nothing. The mock-up of one section takes Chioma about 30 minutes, a small investment for a score-3 prospect.

When a prospect replies with interest, the temptation is to send a price immediately. Pause. A short **qualifying conversation** helps you understand exactly what they need and whether they are a good fit. It saves you from writing proposals for people who cannot pay, cannot decide or do not really need you, and it lets you write a much stronger proposal for those who do.
The BANT checklist

Structure of a 15-minute call

**Open (1 minute):** thank them, confirm the time available, and say what you hope to cover. 'Thanks for your time. I would like to understand what you need, and then suggest whether and how I can help. Does 15 minutes still work?'
**Explore the need (6 minutes):** ask open questions and listen more than you talk.
**Check budget, decider and timing (4 minutes):** use the gentle questions above.
**Summarise (2 minutes):** repeat back what you heard in their words, and ask if you got it right.
**Agree a next step (2 minutes):** for example, 'I will send a short proposal by Friday with two options. Can we speak on Monday to go through it?'

'How are you handling this at the moment?'
'What is not working as well as you would like?'
'What would good look like three months from now?'
'What have you tried before, and what happened?'
'If nothing changes, what does it cost you?'

**Open questions** start with what, how, why or tell me, and cannot be answered with yes or no. Write down the prospect's exact words. When you use their language in your proposal, it shows you listened.

Authority: she asks who decides; he says the proprietor, Mrs Bello, approves anything above ₦50,000 (approximate) and he handles smaller items.
Budget: he has no fixed budget. Halima shares her range: a one-month trial of about ₦45,000, then about ₦80,000 a month (illustrative prices).

Summary: 'So you want more enquiries before admissions in 6 weeks, the page needs to be active again, and Mrs Bello approves larger amounts. Is that right?' He agrees.

Halima proposes the one-month trial, which Mr Bello can approve himself, and asks for a 15-minute meeting with Mrs Bello after the trial to discuss the monthly plan. Need, authority, budget and timing are all clear.
Propose, nurture or let go

After the call, decide. **Propose** if need and authority are clear and budget and timing are close. **Nurture** if there is a real need but the timing is months away: note a follow-up date and send something useful occasionally. **Let go** politely if there is no real need or no way to pay. Letting go is not failure. It frees your time for better prospects.
When the budget is too small

If their budget is far below your price, do not simply cut your fee. Offer a smaller scope instead: 'For about ₦30,000 I could do the menu only, without the photography.' This keeps your hourly value and gives them a real choice.

Quality and Evidence: Follow-up, Honesty and Your Numbers

Most client wins happen after the first message, through polite, well-timed follow-up. This module shows how to follow up without nagging, how to keep your outreach honest and respectful of people's data, and how to measure your pipeline so you improve with evidence instead of guesses.
Follow-up that wins work without nagging
Plan a follow-up sequence with sensible gaps between messages
Add new value in every follow-up instead of 'just checking in'

Silence after your first message rarely means 'no'. Business owners are busy, messages get buried, and decisions get delayed. Many freelancers send one message, hear nothing, and give up, leaving work on the table. A **follow-up sequence** is a planned series of short messages, spaced out over a few weeks, each adding something useful. It shows persistence and professionalism without becoming a nuisance.

**Day 3 or 4, short reminder:** one or two lines that bring your message back to the top. 'Good morning Mr Tamuno, just bringing this back up in case it got buried. Happy to send that menu mock-up if useful.'

**Day 10, useful idea:** send something of value with no strings attached: a quick tip, a relevant example, or the sample you offered. 'Here is a quick mock-up of your starters section, readable on a phone. Feel free to use the idea.'
**Day 21, polite close:** 'I do not want to fill your inbox, so this is my last message for now. If clear menus become a priority, I would be glad to help.'
**Day 60 to 90, check back:** if there is a new trigger (a new branch, a new season), you have a natural reason to return.
Why 'just checking in' fails
A follow-up that only says 'just checking in' asks the reader to do work for you. Each follow-up should give them something: a reminder of the benefit, a sample, an idea, or an easy way to say no.

Would you mind if I share your comment and your restaurant's name with other potential clients?' Keep their reply. Personal data and consent

Your prospect sheet holds personal data: names, phone numbers and notes about people. Nigeria has a data protection law, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). You do not need to be a lawyer to follow its spirit in small-scale outreach. These practical habits are a good starting point:
**Collect fairly:** use contacts published for business purposes or given to you with permission. Do not harvest numbers from private groups or buy contact lists.
**Use for a clear purpose:** contact people about the service you described, not for unrelated things.
**Keep it secure:** protect your phone and sheet with a password, and do not share your prospect list with others.
**Respect requests:** if someone asks you to stop or to delete their details, do it promptly and note the date.
**Get consent for lists:** only add people to WhatsApp broadcast lists or email newsletters if they have agreed.
Larger businesses have more duties

If your business grows to process a lot of personal data, you may have formal duties under the Act. Check the NDPC website or ask a qualified adviser. This lesson covers good practice for small-scale outreach, not legal advice.
Worked example: handling an opt-out properly
For example, Bisi, the Ikeja caterer, sent a personal message to an office manager she found on LinkedIn. The manager replied: 'Please do not contact me again on WhatsApp.'
Bisi replies once: 'Sorry for the disturbance, I will not message again. Have a good week.'
She marks the row 'Do not contact' with the date in her sheet and removes the WhatsApp number.
She removes the contact from her follow-up plan and her WhatsApp Business labels.
Three months later, the same company posts about a staff event. Bisi does not contact the manager. Instead, she lets her inbound channels (her Instagram and Google profile) do the work.
Bisi respected the request completely. Her reputation in the local office community stays clean, which matters more than any single prospect.

Pretending to be a customer to get a business's contact or information.
Messaging the same person on four channels in one day.
Criticising a competitor by name to win the client.
Promising results you do not control, such as sales numbers or government approvals.
Ethical outreach is not slower. Clients who trust you decide faster, pay more reliably and refer others, which you will use in Module 4.

Calculating rates correctly

A rate is one number divided by the number before it, multiplied by 100 to give a percentage. Always divide by the stage just before, not by the total contacted, when you want to find which stage is weak. Keep at least a month of data before drawing conclusions, because small numbers jump around a lot.

For example, Halima, the Kaduna social media manager, tracked her first full month of outreach to schools.

Proposals sent: 4. Proposal rate = 4 / 5 = 80%.
Won: 2. Win rate = 2 / 4 = 50%.
Overall: 2 clients from 40 contacts = 2 / 40 = 5%.
Weakest stage: replies are healthy and proposals win half the time, but only about a third of replies become calls.

Halima's problem is not her first message or her proposals. It is turning replies into calls. She decides to change her reply to interested prospects: instead of 'let me know when you are free', she will offer two specific times.

A 'yes' only matters when it becomes signed, paid work. This module shows how to turn agreement into a clear proposal, deposit and written agreement, how to turn happy clients into referrals and case studies, and how to finish your outreach project with a 90-day plan you can keep running.
From yes to paid: short proposals, deposits and written agreements

Offer two or three options to make deciding easier
Agree payment terms and confirm deposits safely
Confirm the agreement in writing before starting work

Many deals are lost in the gap between 'this sounds good' and actual payment. The prospect is busy, the details are fuzzy, and nobody takes the next step. Your job is to make saying yes simple and clear. For most small service jobs, a **one-page proposal** sent within two working days of your qualifying call, followed by a written confirmation and a deposit, is enough.
What goes in a one-page proposal
**Their situation, in their words:** two sentences from your BANT notes. 'You want more parent enquiries before admissions open in six weeks, and your Facebook page has been quiet since March.'
**What you will do (scope):** a short list of deliverables with quantities. '12 posts over 4 weeks, 2 forwardable admissions flyers, weekly report.'
**What is not included:** prevents disagreement later. 'Paid adverts and printing are not included.'
**Timeline:** start date, key dates and end date.
**Price and payment terms:** total, deposit, balance and when each is due, plus how to pay.
**Next step:** exactly what they do to say yes. 'Reply YES and pay the deposit to start on Monday.'
Give options, not a single take-it-or-leave-it price

Offering two or three options lets the client choose how much to buy, instead of only choosing yes or no. Make the middle option the one you recommend, and make sure each option still pays you properly for the work it includes.
Single price versus options
One price only
Two or three options

No room to adjust

Smaller option keeps talks alive

For example, Bisi, the Ikeja caterer, qualified an insurance broker that holds a monthly staff meeting for 30 people. All prices are illustrative and approximate.
Option A, Basic: jollof rice, chicken and bottled water for 30 at about ₦4,000 per head: 30 x ₦4,000 = ₦120,000.
Option B, Recommended: Option A plus salad, small chops and soft drinks at about ₦5,500 per head: 30 x ₦5,500 = ₦165,000.
Option C, Premium: Option B plus a dessert and two serving staff at about ₦7,000 per head: 30 x ₦7,000 = ₦210,000.
Terms: 50% deposit to confirm the date, balance on delivery day before serving. For Option B, deposit = ₦165,000 x 0.5 = ₦82,500, balance = ₦82,500.
Next step: 'Reply with A, B or C and pay the deposit by Wednesday to confirm Friday 28th.'

The HR officer chose Option B, paid ₦82,500, and Bisi confirmed the transfer in her own banking app before buying ingredients. The client now pays for a better package than the basic one Bisi would have quoted alone.
Deposits and payment safety
Ask for a deposit before you spend money or significant time. Many service providers ask 30% to 50%, depending on how much they must spend upfront.
Accept payment to an account in your business or own name, through bank transfer or a payment link from a provider such as Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint.
Confirm the money has **arrived in your account** in your banking app. Never rely on a screenshot or an SMS 'alert' alone, as both can be faked.
Issue a simple receipt or invoice showing the amount, date, what it is for and the balance due.

Put the agreement in writing

A formal contract drafted by a lawyer is best for large or long jobs. For small jobs, a written confirmation that the client replies to is far better than nothing. Send a short message or email that repeats the chosen option, scope, price, payment terms, dates and what happens if dates change, and ask them to reply 'Confirmed'. Save that reply. If anything goes wrong later, both of you can refer back to what was agreed.
Scope creep

'Can you also just do our logo?' is how small jobs quietly grow into unpaid work. Reply kindly: 'Happy to. A logo is not in our current agreement, so I will send a separate price for it.' The written scope makes this conversation easy.

Finally, send the proposal fast. A proposal sent the same day or the next working day while the conversation is fresh is far more likely to be read than one sent two weeks later. Follow up two working days after sending if you have not heard back.

For larger jobs, long engagements, or work involving a lot of money or sensitive information, ask a lawyer to draft or review a contract. The short written confirmation in this lesson is a practical minimum for small jobs, not a replacement for legal advice on big ones.

Your best source of new clients is often a happy existing client. Referred prospects arrive already trusting you, because someone they respect has vouched for you. But most happy clients do not refer anyone unless asked. This lesson turns referrals and case studies from luck into a habit, and shows you how to communicate the value of your work to clients, mentors and partners.
When and how to ask for a referral

Ask when the client has just seen a result: when they thank you, when you deliver the final work, or when you send a report showing progress. Be **specific** about who you want to meet. 'Do you know anyone who needs my services?' is hard to answer. 'Do you know another school proprietor in Kaduna who is getting ready for admissions?' brings names to mind immediately.
Thank them and mention the result: 'I am so glad the enquiries picked up this term.'
Ask a specific question: 'Do you know one or two other proprietors who might want the same?'
Make it easy: 'If it helps, I can send you a short message you can forward to them.'
Follow up within a day with the forwardable message and thank them again, whatever happens.

Referral partners

A **referral partner** is a business that serves the same clients as you but does not compete with you. A wedding caterer and a decorator, a bookkeeper and a business registration agent, a social media manager and a photographer: each meets clients the other needs. Agree to recommend each other honestly, and only when you would be happy with the other's work. Some partners agree a thank-you fee per referral; if you do, agree it in writing and tell clients if it would affect their trust.
Write a short case study

A **case study** is a short, true story of one job: the client's problem, what you did, and the result. It is the most persuasive proof you can include in outreach and proposals. Keep it to about 120 words, use real numbers where the client agrees, and get permission before naming them. If they prefer privacy, describe them generally, for example 'a 250-pupil school in Kaduna'.
Worked example: Halima's case study
For example, Halima finished the one-month trial with the Kaduna school from Lesson 2.3. She asked Mr Bello's permission to use the school's story and agreed to describe it without the school's name.
Problem: 'A 250-pupil nursery and primary school in Kaduna had an inactive Facebook page and fewer admissions enquiries than the previous term.'
What she did: '12 posts in 4 weeks showing real classroom activities, 2 forwardable admissions flyers, and a weekly report.'
Result, using the school's own records: 'Parent enquiries through WhatsApp rose from 9 in the month before to 23 during the trial month.'
Calculation of change: 23 minus 9 = 14 more enquiries; 14 / 9 = 1.56, about a 156% increase.
Next step: 'The school moved to a monthly plan.'
Honest note: 'Admissions season also played a part; results vary by school.'
Halima now has a 100-word case study with checked numbers, permission and an honest note. She attaches it to every outreach message to other schools.
Only real, checked numbers

Use numbers the client has seen and agreed with, from their own records. Do not round up, do not take credit for results caused by other things, and never invent figures. If you are not sure of a number, describe the change in words instead.
Explaining your process to others

Mentors, business networks and even future employers value someone who can win clients. When you describe your work, be specific about your process and your evidence, not just enthusiastic. Use the pipeline from Lesson 1.1 and your numbers from Lesson 3.3:
Who you target: 'Nursery and primary schools in Kaduna before admissions.'
How you find and reach them: '30 researched prospects a month, personal messages on WhatsApp and email.'
Your results: '40 contacts, 14 replies, 2 new clients last month.'
What you learned and changed: 'I now offer two call times, which increased calls.'
This kind of clear, honest summary also becomes part of your capstone evidence.

Keep a simple 'referrals' column in your sheet showing who referred each new prospect. When a referral becomes a client, send the person who referred them a thank-you message and let them know it worked out. People who feel appreciated tend to refer again.

Building the 90-day plan
Ninety days, about 13 weeks, is long enough to see real results from outreach and short enough to stay focused. Your plan has three parts: a target, weekly actions, and a review rhythm.

Worked example: Ngozi's 90-day plan
For example, Ngozi, the Enugu bookkeeper, has one month of real numbers: 40 contacted, 12 replied (30%), 5 calls, 3 proposals, 2 won. Overall 2 / 40 = 5%. She wants 4 more monthly clients in 90 days.
Target: 4 new clients in 13 weeks.
Contacts needed at her real overall rate of 5%: 4 / 0.05 = 80 contacts.
Weekly contacts: 80 / 13 = 6.2, rounded up to 7 a week, slightly more than one per weekday.
Research: add 8 new prospects a week so the list never runs dry.
Adjustment from her data: her call rate was 5 / 12, about 42%. She will test offering two specific call times in weeks 5 to 8.
Referrals: ask each new client for a specific referral after the first monthly report.
Ngozi's plan asks for about 7 personal messages and 8 new prospects a week, plus one tested change and a referral habit. It is realistic alongside her client work and based on her own numbers.

Many skilled women are very good at their work, but get clients only by chance, then nothing for weeks.
Client acquisition is a separate skill from your service. And like any skill, it can be learned and practised.
It means finding people who need your service, starting conversations with them, and turning the right ones into paying clients.
Inbound means clients come to you. Outbound means you go to them. This course focuses on outbound and referrals, because those are the parts you control.
The pipeline
Five stages from stranger to client
Prospect: a specific business that could need you
Conversation: they have replied, even 'not now'
Qualified: real need, can pay, can decide, soon
Proposal: a clear offer with scope, price, timing
Client: agreed in writing and paid a deposit
Each stage has fewer people, so start with more prospects.
Every client you have ever had passed through five stages. First, a prospect. That is a specific business or person who could need your service.
Second, a conversation. They have replied to you, and a reply of any kind, even 'not now', moves them here.
Third, qualified. You have checked they have a real need, can pay, can decide, and want it soon enough to matter.
Fourth, a proposal. You have sent a clear offer with scope, price and timing.
Fifth, a client. They have agreed in writing and paid a deposit or the full fee.
Each stage has fewer people than the one before, so always start with more prospects than the clients you want.

Qualify before you price
BANT: four things to find out
When someone replies with interest, do not rush to send a price. Hold a short qualifying call first, using a checklist called BANT.
Budget. Ask gently, 'Have you set aside a budget, or would it help if I shared typical ranges?'
Authority. 'Apart from you, who else will be involved in deciding?'
Need. 'What is happening now that made you interested?' Listen more than you talk, and write down her exact words.
Timeline. 'When would you like this in place?' If you cannot tick at least need and authority, you are not ready to propose.

Silence after your first message rarely means no. Business owners are busy, and messages get buried.

Follow-up sequence
Four touches, spaced out
Day 0: your four-part first message
Day 3 or 4: a short reminder
Day 10: a useful idea, no strings
Day 21: a polite close
Day 60 to 90: check back with a new trigger
Every follow-up adds value. Never just 'checking in'.
Day 0 is your first message.
On day 3 or 4, send one or two lines that bring it back to the top.
On day 10, send something useful with no strings attached, like a tip or the sample you offered.
On day 21, close politely. Say this is your last message for now, and that you would be glad to help later.
After 60 to 90 days, a new trigger like a new branch gives you a natural reason to return.
'Just checking in' asks the reader to do work for you. Each message should give her something.

For example, Ngozi, the bookkeeper, messages a pharmacy owner on 3 March. No reply.

Why this matters

A yes only matters when it becomes signed, paid work. Many deals are lost in the gap between 'this sounds good' and actual payment.
Your job is to make saying yes simple and clear.
Then you turn happy clients into referrals and short case studies.
And you finish with a 90-day plan, because freelancers most often run out of work when they stop outreach while busy.
One-page proposal
Six parts of your proposal
Their situation, in their own words
What you will do, with quantities
What is not included
Timeline: start, key dates, end
Price, deposit, balance and how to pay
Next step: exactly how to say yes
Send a one-page proposal within two working days of your call. Start with her situation, in her own words from your BANT notes.
List what you will do, with quantities, like 12 posts over 4 weeks.
Say what is not included. This prevents disagreement later.
Give the start date, key dates and end date.
State the total, the deposit, the balance, and when each is due.
And end with one clear next step, such as 'Reply YES and pay the deposit to start on Monday.'
Give options
Bisi's three-option catering proposal
For example, Bisi, a caterer in Ikeja, quotes an office meeting for 30 people.
A, Basic: 30 x 4,000
B, Recommended: 30 x 5,500
C, Premium: 30 x 7,000
Deposit for B, 50%
Naira prices are approximate and illustrative.
A single price makes the client decide yes or no. Two or three options make her decide which one, and your rate stays the same.
Option A is jollof rice, chicken and water, at about 4,000 naira per head. That is 120,000 naira.
Option B, the recommended one, adds salad, small chops and soft drinks, at about 5,500 naira per head. 165,000 naira.
Option C adds dessert and two serving staff, at about 7,000 naira per head. 210,000 naira.
The HR officer chose Option B and paid a 50% deposit of 82,500 naira. She now buys a better package than the basic one Bisi would have quoted alone.
Money safety
Deposit of 30% to 50% before you spend
Paid into an account in your own name
Confirmed in your own banking app
Receipt with amount, date and balance
Client replies 'Confirmed' in writing
Ask for a deposit before you spend money or much time. Many providers ask 30% to 50%.
Bisi confirmed the transfer in her own banking app before buying ingredients. Never rely on a screenshot or SMS alert, because both can be faked.
Send a written confirmation of the scope, price and dates, and ask the client to reply 'Confirmed'. If she later asks you to 'just do our logo', kindly send a separate price.
Referrals
Ask for a referral the right way
Ask right after a visible result
Thank her and mention the result
Offer a message she can forward
Thank her again, whatever happens
Most happy clients never refer anyone unless you ask. Ask when she has just seen a result.
Thank her and mention the result.
Then be specific. 'Do you know anyone who needs my services?' is hard to answer. 'Do you know another school proprietor in Kaduna getting ready for admissions?' brings names to mind.
Offer a short message she can forward, so referring you takes seconds. Then thank her again, whatever happens.
Case study
Halima's honest case study
Problem: inactive page, fewer enquiries
Did: 12 posts in 4 weeks, 2 flyers
Result: enquiries rose from 9 to 23
Honest note: admissions season helped too
Only real numbers the client has seen and agreed.
A case study is a short, true story of one job. For example, Halima asked permission, then described a 250-pupil school in Kaduna with an inactive Facebook page.
She wrote what she did: 12 posts in 4 weeks, and 2 forwardable flyers.
Using the school's own records, parent enquiries rose from 9 to 23 during the trial month.
And she added an honest note: admissions season also played a part.
Never round up or invent figures. If you are not sure of a number, describe the change in words.
Ngozi plans from her real numbers
Real overall rate: 2 clients from 40, 5%
Target: 4 new clients in 13 weeks
80 contacts, about 7 a week
Add 8 new prospects a week
Review at weeks 4 and 8; test one change
For example, Ngozi's first real month gave her 2 clients from 40 contacts. That is 5%.
She wants 4 more monthly clients in 90 days, about 13 weeks.
At 5%, she needs 80 contacts. That is about 7 personal messages a week.
She adds 8 new prospects every week so her list never runs dry.
She reviews at weeks 4 and 8, and tests one change: offering two specific call times. Even in busy weeks, keep the Friday update and a few messages, because pipelines take weeks to refill.
